'''''Freesia leichtlinii''''' is a species of herb in the family [[Iridaceae]], native to the Cape Provinces of South Africa.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Freesia leichtlinii Klatt - Encyclopedia of Life|url=https://eol.org/pages/5866057|access-date=2022-02-04|website=eol.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Mifsud |first=Stephen |date=2002-08-23 |title=Freesia leichtlinii (Leichtlin's Freesia) : MaltaWildPlants.com - the online Flora of the Maltese Islands. |url=https://www.maltawildplants.com/IRID/Freesia_leichtlinii.php |access-date=2022-03-03 |website=www.maltawildplants.com |language=en-us}}</ref> It is most widely known in its subspecies F. leichtlinii subsp. alba, commonly called [[Freesia alba|Antique White Freesia]], which has naturalized in California, the Mediterranean Basin, and parts of the Southern Hemisphere.

== Taxonomy and Nomenclature ==
The genus ''Freesia'' was first described as a distinct genus in 1866 by Christian Friedrich Ecklon and named in honor of Friedrich Heinrich Theodor Freese (died 1876), a German physician and student of South African plants. The epithet leichtlinii was named for [[Max Leichtlin]], a German horticulturalist and plant collector active in the nineteenth century.<ref name=":0">Manning, J.C. & Goldblatt, P. (2010). ''Botany and Horticulture of the Genus Freesia (Iridaceae)''. Strelitzia 27. South African National Biodiversity Institute, Pretoria.</ref> In 2010 [[Freesia alba]] was consolidated into ''F. leichtlinii'' as a subspecies, creating the binomial ''Freesia leichtlinii subsp. alba''.<ref name=":0" />

== Toxicity ==
No part of the plant is considered harmful for human contact or ingestion. Freesia is listed by the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (ASPCA) among plants that are generally safe for dogs and cats. However, ingestion of the above-ground parts (leaves, stems, flowers) may cause mild gastrointestinal upset in sensitive animals.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Toxic and Non-Toxic Plants |url=https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/aspca-poison-control/toxic-and-non-toxic-plants |access-date=2026-03-30 |website=www.aspca.org |language=en}}</ref> The corms are more irritating than the above-ground portions and can cause more significant gastrointestinal distress if consumed. Pet owners are advised to discourage animals from digging up and chewing on corms.<ref name=":1" />
